changelog.change: Initial entry — converted from the CV Difficult Airway guide. The anatomically/procedurally difficult airway and the failed-airway algorithm (DAS 2025 Plans A-D, the Vortex, eFONA technique, human factors). Companion to the physiologically-difficult-airway module.

summary: Once Plan A fails, the outcome depends on which of three states you are in — tube in, or failed-but-oxygenating, or can't-intubate-can't-oxygenate — not on trying the same thing harder. DAS 2025 keeps a linear A→B→C→D structure and, new for 2025, puts the supraglottic airway ahead of face mask as Plan B. The lethal errors are behavioural: perseveration on a failed technique, not saying the words 'this is a CICO emergency', and reluctance to cut.

body.text: Three outcomes of every emergency intubation

items: Plan A works — video laryngoscopy with a stylet, tube in. ~85% of the time with VL.
Plan A fails but you can oxygenate (BVM or SGA). You have time. Stop, think, regroup — do not immediately reinsert the blade.
Nothing works and you cannot oxygenate — can't intubate, can't oxygenate (CICO). The emergency inside the emergency; it occurs in ~0.5% of difficult airways.

body.text: Key 2025 paradigm shift: maximise first-attempt success — don't just manage failure after it happens. The order also changed from 2015: the SGA is now Plan B, ahead of face mask, reflecting its reliability as a rescue device.
Anticipate — before you push the drugs

The best time to identify a difficult airway is before induction. The MACOCHA score (0-12) was built for the ICU: Mallampati III/IV (5), OSA (2), reduced cervical-spine mobility (1), mouth opening < 3 cm (1), coma/GCS < 8 (1), SpO₂ < 80% (1), non-anaesthesiologist operator (1). A score ≥ 3 predicts a difficult intubation — verbalise it and prepare for it. But anticipation is imperfect: in the ID-ACCT cohort 16% of ICU patients had a known difficult airway and only 29% of those were clearly identifiable at the bedside. If MACOCHA is high and CICO risk is high, consider an awake technique.
Plan A — make the first attempt the best attempt

items: Video laryngoscopy first-line for most intubations, not only anticipated difficult ones (DEVICE, n=1,417 across 17 EDs/ICUs: first-pass 85.1% VL vs 70.8% DL, P < 0.001).
Positioning: ear to sternal notch, head of bed elevated.
Full neuromuscular blockade confirmed before the blade goes in — a tense patient defeats both laryngoscopy and mask ventilation.
Styletted ETT, bougie in hand, suction running, EtCO₂ connected.
Best available operator takes the first attempt.

body.text: Each failed attempt roughly doubles the complication rate. First-pass success is the goal; everything after it is rescue.
Plan A fails — the most important 10 seconds

First attempt failed, SpO₂ is holding. Before touching the blade again, answer three questions: (1) Can I oxygenate? BVM or SGA — if yes, you have time. (2) Why did it fail? View, tube delivery, secretions? (3) What will I change? Different blade, a bougie, or a different operator.

The 3-attempt rule (CAFG): a maximum of 3 total intubation attempts, each meaningfully different from the last. After 3, declare failed intubation and move to Plan B. Repeating the same technique hoping for a different result is perseveration — that is how people die.
Plan B — supraglottic airway

items: Failed intubation but you can oxygenate: place a second-generation SGA (i-gel, LMA Supreme) — better seal and a gastric drainage port.
Ventilate through it while you regroup; it buys time and restores oxygenation.
You can intubate through it — pass a flexible bronchoscope-guided tube through the SGA. Know how before you need it.
Call for help: anaesthesia, ENT, whoever your institution's airway expert is.
The SGA is not a failure — it is a lifeline. Use it.

body.text: Plan C — face mask: the fork in the road

items: If the SGA fails, optimise face-mask ventilation: two-person technique (one seals, one squeezes), jaw thrust, head tilt, OPA and/or NPA.
Confirm neuromuscular blockade — a tense patient makes mask ventilation impossible.

The decision point: can you oxygenate via face mask? YES → you have time; regroup, call for help, consider bronchoscopic intubation through an SGA, an awake approach, or elective FONA. NO → this is a CICO emergency. Declare it — say the words out loud.

body.text: Plan D — CICO → eFONA

Cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate. Three things happen simultaneously: (1) declare CICO out loud so everyone in the room hears it; (2) confirm or establish full neuromuscular blockade — give rocuronium if not already paralysed; (3) one final attempt at any untried technique, only if it genuinely has not been tried. If that fails: scalpel to neck, immediately, no more delays.

eFONA — scalpel, bougie, tube (DAS 2025 / CAFG / ASA):
1. Stabilise the larynx with the non-dominant hand.
2. Vertical skin incision ~4 cm over the cricothyroid membrane.
3. Horizontal stab through the cricothyroid membrane.
4. Turn the scalpel 90°, sharp edge caudal, maintain traction.
5. Slide the bougie through the incision, feeling for tracheal-ring clicks.
6. Railroad a 6.0 cuffed ETT over the bougie.
7. Inflate the cuff, confirm with EtCO₂, secure.
Equipment: #20 scalpel, bougie, 6.0 cuffed ETT, 10 mL syringe. Scalpel-bougie-tube beats a cannula technique under stress (83% vs 18% rescue oxygenation through thick pretracheal tissue in a porcine model) — it is a definitive airway immediately with fewer failure points.
The Vortex — a crisis mental model

items: Green zone: the patient is oxygenated — you are safe. Everything you do aims to get back here.
The funnel has three lifelines back to green: ETT, SGA, face mask. Each gets one best effort; if it fails, move to the next.
Bottom of the funnel: all three lifelines exhausted → CICO → eFONA.
The Vortex does not tell you how to intubate — it tells you when to stop trying and move on, which is the part clinicians are worst at.

body.text: Human factors — the errors that actually kill

items: Perseveration: repeating the same failed technique 4, 5, 6 times.
Failure to declare CICO: everyone knows it is a crisis but nobody says the words.
Reluctance to cut: 'I've never done a cric', so you keep trying things that are not working. NAP4 found delayed or omitted cricothyrotomy was a recurring theme in airway-related ICU deaths.
Escalation is not failure — it is adaptation under pressure. DAS 2025 (via a Safety-II reading) explicitly legitimises escalation as an adaptive response.

body.text: The team brief — out loud before every intubation (~30 s)

"This is a low / moderate / high-risk airway. Plan A is video laryngoscopy with a stylet; bougie is at the bedside. Plan B is the i-gel, sized by ideal body weight. Plan C is face-mask ventilation. Plan D is a surgical airway; the cric kit is on the cart. We have all our equipment and adjuncts at hand. Any questions before we start?"
Cheat sheet

rows: MACOCHA score. ≥ 3 → prepare for difficulty. High CICO risk → consider awake intubation.
VL with stylet, bougie at hand. Optimise positioning, NMB, suction. Best operator. Max 3 attempts, each different.
SGA (i-gel / LMA). Ventilate, regroup. Consider bronchoscopic intubation through the SGA.
Face-mask ventilation. Two-person technique. OPA/NPA. Optimise NMB. Ask: can I oxygenate?
Declare it out loud. Confirm NMB. One final untried technique. Then scalpel-bougie-tube, now.

body.text: The algorithm is not a flowchart to memorise — it is a mental model so that when Plan A fails, and eventually it will, you do not freeze: Anticipate (MACOCHA) → Optimise (first-pass success) → Recognise failure (3-attempt rule) → Rescue (SGA → BVM) → Escalate (eFONA).
